The FootNet LSTM classifies each frame of a running video as ground contact or flight.
The per-frame binary contact signal yields strikefoot events (rising edges) and ground contact time.
The FootNet model is a bidirectional 2-layer LSTM with 32 hidden units and a single sigmoid output per timestep.
The LSTM input at each timestep is a 4-feature vector.
Horizontal ankle velocity captures forward and backward movement of the ankle.
Vertical ankle velocity captures up and down movement of the ankle.
Shin velocity is the x-velocity of the ankle-to-knee vector.
Tibial angle is the angle of the shin relative to vertical.
The four LSTM features and the bidirectional architecture are adapted from the original FootNet paper on foot-strike and toe-off detection.

Rivadulla et al. (2021) developed and validated FootNet, a kinematic algorithm to improve foot-strike and toe-off detection in treadmill running, published in PLoS One (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0248608).
The original FootNet paper's inputs are derived from motion capture.
FootNet's motion-capture inputs are distal tibia anteroposterior velocity, ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion angle, and foot centre-of-mass anteroposterior and vertical velocities.
StrideLens approximates FootNet's motion-capture signals using YOLO pose keypoints.
Ankle X and Y velocity serves as a proxy for foot centre-of-mass velocity.
Shin velocity serves as a proxy for tibial velocity.
Tibial angle serves as a proxy for ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
The underlying biomechanical signals are the same as FootNet; only the measurement modality differs.
The original FootNet paper uses 400 hidden units per LSTM layer and a 200-node dense layer.
The StrideLens implementation uses 32 hidden units with no intermediate dense layer.
The capacity reduction is intentional because the training dataset is small (17 videos) and a paper-scale model would severely overfit.
32 hidden units was chosen to match model capacity to dataset size.
The four features capture the characteristic ankle deceleration, anterior tibial rotation, and shin angle change that occur at the moment of ground contact.
These discriminative signals were validated in the FootNet paper across 70 participants and 5 independent datasets.
Rivadulla et al. show that bidirectional LSTMs outperform unidirectional ones for contact detection.
The bidirectional architecture helps because the approach phase immediately before contact is as informationally rich as the contact frame itself.
Contact frames are a minority of total frames in any running video, creating class imbalance.
A contact threshold of 0.35 rather than 0.5 compensates for the model's tendency to underpredict contact.
The FootNet model was trained on fixed-length gait cycles resampled to 40 frames.
At inference, gait cycle boundaries are unknown, so overlapping sliding windows with a majority vote replicate the training distribution.
Overstriding is detected by computing the horizontal distance between the ankle at initial contact and a vertical line dropped from the estimated centre of mass.
Initial contact frames for overstriding are supplied by the FootNet LSTM output.
Overstriding distance is measured at the exact frame of initial contact, the rising edge of the FootNet contact signal.
The ankle joint centre is approximated by the lateral malleolus.
The centre of mass is estimated as the midpoint of the left and right hip keypoints, the greater trochanter approximation.
A positive overstride value means the ankle is ahead of the centre of mass, the typical direction for overstriding.
A negative overstride value means the ankle is behind the centre of mass.
An ankle 0 to 5 cm ahead of the centre of mass is an optimal landing with minimal braking impulse and knee flexion to absorb load.
An ankle 5 to 10 cm ahead of the centre of mass is a mild overstride where the leg begins acting as a rigid strut with elevated patellofemoral loading.
An ankle more than 10 cm ahead of the centre of mass is a severe overstride with a backward-directed braking impulse and high tibial and knee stress.
Sprinters occasionally land 20 to 30 cm ahead of the centre of mass, but only at maximal velocity where ground contact time is extremely short.
For recreational and distance running, the 5 to 6 cm threshold is the standard clinical overstriding cutoff.
The overstriding thresholds are expressed in centimetres.
Until pixel-to-metre calibration is implemented, the computed overstride distance is in pixels and cannot be compared against the centimetre thresholds.
Calibration using the athlete's reported height and the hip-to-ankle pixel distance as a scale factor is the planned approach.
The shin test is the sagittal-plane complement to the centre-of-mass test.
Centre-of-mass distance captures the braking cost of overstriding, whereas tibia or shank angle captures the skeletal stress.
The tibia angle indicates whether the knee is positioned to flex and absorb impact or is extended into a rigid strut.
Both the centre-of-mass test and the shin test are read at the same frame, initial contact.
The tibia angle is measured between the shin segment, from ankle to knee keypoints, and true vertical.
A backward-leaning shin with the knee behind the ankle at contact means the leg lands extended, removing the knee's shock-absorbing flexion.
A tibia lean from 0 to minus 4 degrees, or any forward angle, is considered safe, with the knee flexing under a slightly bent leg so muscle absorbs shock.
A tibia lean from minus 5 to minus 9 degrees is a mild band where the shin leans back and shock shifts from muscle to joint.
A tibia lean of minus 10 degrees or more backward is a severe band where the knee is near-locked and the leg acts as a rigid pillar.
The centre-of-mass and tibia tests fail independently, so the report logic can cross-reference them.
An optimal profile has a centre-of-mass distance of 0 to 5 cm and a tibia of 0 to minus 4 degrees, indicating a foot near the pelvis and a compliant knee with the lowest injury risk and best economy.
An efficient but volatile profile lands close, at 2 to 5 cm, but with the knee snapped straight at minus 10 degrees or more, risking localised bone stress in the shin or heel.
An inefficient but protected profile reaches out front at 12 cm or more but keeps the knee bent at 0 to minus 4 degrees, risking metabolic drain and early muscle fatigue.
A high-threat profile combines an extended leg and locked knee, at 12 cm or more and minus 10 degrees or more, with heel strike, risking tibial stress fracture, shin splints, and runner's knee.
Raising cadence 5 to 10 percent is the single intervention that improves both the centre-of-mass and tibia axes at once.
Raising cadence shortens the reach and rotates the shin toward vertical without the runner consciously changing foot placement.
The degree and centimetre bands are clinical screening heuristics from physiotherapy practice, not validated categorical cutoffs.
Peer-reviewed evidence warns against treating landing angles as clean bins.
Stiffler-Joachim et al. (2019) show the foot-angle to vertical-loading-rate relationship is nonlinear, with a cubic fit significantly better than linear.
Vertical loading rate is actually lowest at the angular extremes and highest in the mid-range.
A monotonic more-backward-is-worse rule misrepresents the mechanics.
StrideLens should store and report the continuous tibia angle and use the bands only as coarse screening flags.
Barrett et al. (2023) published Implementation of 2D Running Gait Analysis in Orthopedic Physical Therapy Clinics in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (doi:10.26603/001c.74726).
Barrett et al. is a RE-AIM implementation and feasibility study showing orthopedic physical therapy clinics can adopt a 2D running gait analysis protocol in routine practice.
Barrett et al. supports the real-world clinical use of single-camera side-view 2D gait analysis as a screening instrument.
Barrett et al. documents adoption and clinician-perceived usefulness, not measurement validity against 3D.

Edwards et al. (2009) published Effects of Stride Length and Running Mileage on a Probabilistic Stress Fracture Model in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181a984c4).
Edwards et al. showed that a 10 percent reduction in stride length lowers the probability of tibial stress fracture by 3 to 6 percent.
Edwards et al. grounds the mechanical link between longer stride reach, or overstriding, and tibial bone stress.
Edwards et al. manipulates stride length rather than foot-to-centre-of-mass distance directly, so it supports the risk framing rather than a specific centimetre cutoff.
Heiderscheit et al. (2011) published Effects of Step Rate Manipulation on Joint Mechanics during Running in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e3181ebedf5).
Heiderscheit et al. demonstrated that increasing cadence by 5 to 10 percent significantly reduces the horizontal distance between the foot and the centre of mass at initial contact.
Reducing the foot-to-centre-of-mass distance via higher cadence reduces joint loading at the hip and knee.
Heiderscheit et al. grounds cadence as the primary exercise intervention recommended when overstriding is flagged.
Increasing step rate is the most evidence-backed cue for reducing overstride distance without changing conscious foot placement.

Martinez et al. (2022) published Comparison of 2-D and 3-D Analysis of Running Kinematics and Actual Versus Predicted Running Kinetics in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (doi:10.26603/001c.34432).
Martinez et al. validates that 2D sagittal-plane video approximates 3D running kinematics, with mean 2D-to-3D differences of only about 1 to 3 degrees for shank and leg segment angles.
Martinez et al. shows regression equations predict 3D kinetics, including vertical ground reaction force with an R-squared of 0.75 and average loading rate with an R-squared of 0.52.

Martinez et al. provides the methodological justification for the single-camera approach, showing phone sagittal keypoints are sufficient to estimate the braking and loading quantities that overstriding drives.
Napier et al. (2018) published Kinetic Risk Factors of Running-Related Injuries in Female Recreational Runners in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine and Science in Sports (doi:10.1111/sms.13228).
Napier et al. identified peak braking, or anterior-posterior, force as the strongest kinetic predictor of running-related injury.
In Napier et al., runners in the highest braking-force tertile were injured at roughly 5 to 8 times the rate of the lower tertiles.
Because braking impulse scales with how far the foot lands ahead of the centre of mass, Napier et al. grounds the overstride-distance metric in injury epidemiology.
Napier et al. justifies flagging the mild 5 to 10 cm overstride range rather than treating it as acceptable.
Souza (2016) published An Evidence-Based Videotaped Running Biomechanics Analysis in Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Clinics of North America (doi:10.1016/j.pmr.2015.08.006).
Souza is the primary clinical source for the shin test.

Souza establishes tibia angle at loading response, alongside foot inclination angle and knee flexion at initial contact, as a sagittal-plane indicator of overstriding when force plates are unavailable.
Souza states that an extended tibia is not ideal, whereas a vertical or flexed tibia allows the runner to dissipate impact through knee flexion.
In Souza, knee flexion under about 45 degrees suggests reduced shock absorption.

Stiffler-Joachim et al. (2019) published Foot Angle and Loading Rate during Running Demonstrate a Nonlinear Relationship in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise (doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002023).
In Stiffler-Joachim et al., foot inclination angle and average vertical loading rate follow a cubic rather than linear relationship.
Stiffler-Joachim et al. found vertical loading rate lowest at the angular extremes.
Stiffler-Joachim et al. warns that binning landing angles into categories may misrepresent the relationship.
Stiffler-Joachim et al. grounds the decision to report the continuous tibia angle rather than treat the screening bands as hard cutoffs.
The FootNet contact detection is implemented in ml/src/models/footnet_model.py and ml/src/inference/footnet_inference.py.
Overstriding detection is planned for ml/src/inference/inference_metrics.py.
